'''''Plumeria obtusa''''', the '''Singapore graveyard flower''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PLOB2|taxon=Plumeria obtusa|accessdate=8 October 2015}}</ref> is a species of the genus ''[[Plumeria]]'' ([[Apocynaceae]]). It is native to the [[Neotropical realm|Neotropics]], but widely cultivated for its ornamental and fragrant flowers around the world, where suitably warm climate exists.
[[File:Plumeria obtusa or the Singapore graveyard flower (Image 1 of 2) in Jamshedpur, India.jpg|thumb|Closeup of Singapore graveyard flower in [[Jamshedpur]]]]

==Taxonomy==
''Plumeria obtusa'' was [[species description|described]] as a new species in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.marinespecies.org/aphia.php?p=taxdetails&id=418749| title=Plumeria obtusa Linnaeus, 1753|website=WoRMS| access-date=3 October 2019|date=6 October 2009}}</ref> Its [[specific epithet (botany)|specific epithet]] "''obtusa''" means "blunt", in reference to its blunt-tipped leaves.<ref name="MBG"/>

==Description==
''Plumeria obtusa'' is a small tree, growing {{cvt|10-15|ft|m|order=flip}} tall. Infrequently, individuals can grow to be {{cvt|25|ft|m|order=flip}}. Its flowers are white with yellow throats and each has five petals. The fragrant flowers bloom in clusters. Leaves are dark green, glossy, and up to {{cvt|8|in|cm|order=flip}} long. They are obovate, or teardrop-shaped.<ref name="MBG">{{cite web|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=f412| title=Plumeria obtusa| website=Missouri Botanical Garden| access-date=3 October 2019}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Plumeria obtusa'' is native to the [[West Indies]] (including the [[The Bahamas|Bahamas]] and the [[Greater Antilles]]), southern [[Mexico]], [[Belize]], and [[Guatemala]].<ref>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=161613 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref name="Plumeria obtusa">{{GRIN|accessdate=2009-02-01}}</ref>  Cultivation is common in warmer parts of the world, including [[Florida]], [[Southeast Asia]], and coastal parts of the [[Arabian Peninsula]]. It is reportedly naturalized in [[China]] and [[India]].<ref name="dyphon">Dy Phon Pauline, 2000, ''Plants Used In Cambodia'', printed by Imprimierie Olympic, Phnom Penh</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Plumeria obtusa in Flora of China @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=210001685 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref>

==Common names==
* ''châmpéi slük tiel''  - [[Khmer language|Khmer]]<ref name=dyphon />
* ''gulcampā'' - [[Maldivian language|Dhivehi]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sujanapal |first=P. |url=https://www.fao.org/3/i5777e/i5777e.pdf |title=Common Plants of Maldives |last2=Sancaran |first2=K.V. |publisher=[[Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations]] and [[Kerala Forest Research Institute]] |year=2016 |isbn=978-92-5-109295-8 |location=[[Bangkok]] |page=212}}</ref>

==Uses==
This plant is commonly used as an ornamental, grown for its flowers. In Cambodia the flowers are used to make necklaces and in offerings to the deities.<ref name=dyphon /> In traditional medicine used in that country, a decoction of the bark is given in varying doses as a purgative or as a remedy against oedema.
